text: You think of GE as light bulbs and jet engines. But in two thousand eight, the thing that nearly broke it was a bank you never saw. On October first, two thousand eight, General Electric agreed to sell three billion dollars of special stock to Warren Buffett, at a ten percent dividend. Six weeks later, its finance arm was approved for a government guarantee on up to a hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars of debt. It also borrowed sixteen billion dollars through an emergency program run by the Federal Reserve. By March, the government was standing behind almost seventy-four billion dollars of GE's borrowing. And the stock had fallen to six dollars and sixty-six cents. So how does a company that builds jet engines end up there?

The answer is a bank that lived inside GE for seventy-six years. It made GE one of the most valuable companies on Earth. Then it nearly took the whole company down. We're going to follow that bank, from a small finance office in the Great Depression to the weeks in two thousand eight when its lenders hesitated. One thing up front. Every program GE used in the crisis was legal, and open to companies that qualified. This isn't a fraud story. It's a story about how money works, and what happens when it stops. Every number on screen comes from a filing, a regulator, or a named report. The sources are in the description.

It starts in nineteen thirty-two. America is deep in the Depression, and GE has a problem. People want its fridges and appliances, but they can't pay all at once. So GE sets up a small finance arm. Its job is simple. Lend customers the money to buy GE products, and get paid back a little each month. In nineteen forty-three, it becomes General Electric Capital Corporation. For decades it stays a helper, there to help GE sell more things. Then it starts lending to almost anyone. Loans and leases for businesses. Office towers and real estate. Consumer loans, credit cards, even bank accounts. It didn't need to sell a single GE product to make money anymore. By the end of two thousand seven, GE's financial services business holds six hundred and forty-six billion dollars of assets. By the middle of two thousand eight, six hundred and ninety-six billion. And it earns twelve point four billion dollars that year. GE as a whole earned twenty-two point two billion. So more than half of the profit of America's great industrial company came from its bank. On paper, it was beautiful. The factories brought the brand and the credit rating. The bank turned that credit rating into profit. Wall Street loved it. In August two thousand, GE was worth about six hundred billion dollars. But how does a finance arm grow that big that fast? The secret was not what it lent. It was how it borrowed.

GE had a top credit rating, triple A. That let GE Capital borrow money more cheaply than almost anyone. And much of that borrowing was commercial paper. Think of it as a short IOU. Big investors, like money market funds, lend you cash for a few days or a few weeks. When the IOU comes due, you pay it back by selling a new one. As long as investors keep buying, the money rolls over forever. Cheap, short money, lent out as long loans that take years to pay back. Here's the catch. A long loan can't be called back early. A short IOU has to be repaid on its date. So the bank has to find new lenders on schedule, every few weeks, in good times and in bad. GE became the largest issuer of commercial paper in the United States. At one point in two thousand eight, it had almost a hundred billion dollars outstanding. That is a lot of money that has to be borrowed again, every few weeks. Now picture September two thousand eight. On the fifteenth, Lehman Brothers collapses. Investors start asking which big borrower might be next. According to the memoir of Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, GE's chief executive Jeff Immelt called him on September eighth about trouble selling commercial paper, and they spoke again on the fifteenth. GE disputes that account. Its own letter to investors on September fourteenth said its commercial paper programs remained robust. But either way, the question was now in the air. What happens if the lenders stop rolling over?

On October first, GE answers with a show of strength. Warren Buffett's company, Berkshire Hathaway, agrees to buy three billion dollars of GE preferred stock. It pays a ten percent dividend. That's three hundred million dollars a year. GE can buy it back after three years, but only at a ten percent premium. Buffett also gets warrants: the right to buy about a hundred and thirty-five million GE shares at twenty-two dollars and twenty-five cents each, for five years. Those are the terms of a lender who knows he is needed. On the same day, GE says it will sell at least twelve billion dollars of new shares to the public. Within a week it's done. Five hundred and forty-seven million shares, sold at twenty-two dollars and twenty-five cents. About fifteen billion dollars of fresh capital in one week. And the stock offering means every existing shareholder now owns a smaller slice of GE. For the record, the deal worked out well for Buffett. In two thousand eleven, GE bought the stock back for three point three billion dollars, after paying about nine hundred million dollars in dividends. But in October two thousand eight, for a company that had always looked unbreakable, it was a signal. And it still wasn't enough.

In October, Paulson writes, Immelt told him: we need help. That month, the government was building a safety net. The FDIC would guarantee new debt issued by banks, so lenders would keep lending. There was one problem. GE Capital wasn't a traditional bank. Under the first rules, it didn't qualify. A guarantee means this: if GE Capital couldn't pay a lender back, the FDIC would. Then the rules changed. On November twelfth, GE said GE Capital had been approved for the program, for up to a hundred and thirty-nine billion dollars of debt. At the same time, the Federal Reserve was running its own rescue for the commercial paper market. The idea was simple. If investors wouldn't buy a company's short IOUs, the Fed's own program would. Over several weeks in late two thousand eight, GE borrowed sixteen billion dollars through it. It wasn't alone. Eighty-two companies borrowed through that program, seven hundred and thirty-eight billion dollars in all. But look at the guarantee. At the end of two thousand eight, thirty-five point two billion dollars of GE Capital's debt carried the FDIC's backing. Three months later, seventy-three point nine nine billion. GE Capital became the largest user of the program. In December, GE set a new goal: cut its commercial paper to fifty billion dollars in two thousand nine. Under the deal, GE had to pay the FDIC back for any money it ever paid out on that debt. But for those months, the government's name stood behind the bank inside GE.

Then came the bill. For two thousand eight, the financial business still earned seven point eight billion dollars. But a year earlier it had earned twelve point four, and investors could see where the losses were coming from. On February twenty-seventh, two thousand nine, GE cut its quarterly dividend from thirty-one cents to ten cents. It was GE's first dividend cut since nineteen thirty-eight. It saved about nine billion dollars a year. On March fifth, the stock closed at six dollars and sixty-six cents. Remember Buffett's price? Twenty-two dollars and twenty-five cents. A week later, Standard and Poor's took away GE's triple A rating. The thing that made the money cheap was gone. So GE started to shrink the machine. Commercial paper went from seventy-one point eight billion dollars at the end of two thousand eight, to forty-seven point three billion a year later. In two thousand thirteen, regulators named GE Capital systemically important. Their concern was the same one: it leaned on short-term funding. And in April two thousand fifteen, GE gave up. It announced it would sell most of GE Capital, about two hundred billion dollars of it, within two years. Real estate went first, much of it to funds managed by Blackstone, in deals worth about twenty-six and a half billion dollars. The first charge was about sixteen billion dollars. In two thousand fourteen, only fifty-eight percent of GE's earnings came from its industrial businesses. The plan was to make that more than ninety percent by twenty eighteen. Investors cheered. The stock rose eleven percent that day. A year later, in June two thousand sixteen, regulators voted unanimously that GE Capital was small enough. The Federal Reserve would no longer supervise it. It had cut its assets by more than half. It was the first time that label had ever been removed. It looked like the story was over. It wasn't.

Inside what was left of GE Capital sat an old insurance business. It had taken on long-term care policies from other insurers, mostly written between nineteen eighty-nine and two thousand six. These policies pay for nursing homes and home care, often decades after they are sold. So nobody knows the real cost until years later. In two thousand eighteen, GE found out its old estimates were too low. In January two thousand eighteen, GE announced the bill. A six point two billion dollar charge after tax. And about fifteen billion dollars it would have to put into the insurance business over seven years. About three billion right away, then about two billion every year through twenty twenty-four. And GE Capital would stop paying dividends to its parent. By then, the dividend had already been halved, in November two thousand seventeen, to twelve cents. In June two thousand eighteen, GE was removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It had been a member continuously since nineteen oh seven. In October, a new chief executive, Larry Culp, cut the dividend again, to one cent a share. That quarter, GE reported a loss of twenty-two point eight billion dollars, mostly from writing down its power business. By January two thousand nineteen, GE was worth about seventy-five billion dollars. At its peak it had been worth about six hundred billion. In two thousand twenty, the SEC fined GE two hundred million dollars. It said GE had not told investors that a large part of its power profits came from lowering earlier cost estimates, and that it had lowered expected insurance claim costs without explaining the uncertainty. GE neither admitted nor denied those findings, and it did not have to restate its results.

So what happened to the company itself? GE broke itself up. GE HealthCare was spun off in January two thousand twenty-three. GE Vernova, the power business, followed in April two thousand twenty-four. What remained became GE Aerospace. And here is the twist. GE Vernova builds gas turbines. And the AI boom needs power. In the third quarter of twenty twenty-six, GE Vernova took twenty-nine point three billion dollars of orders. Its backlog reached a hundred and ninety-seven billion dollars. Its gas turbine backlog and reservations reached a hundred and twenty-two gigawatts, and it expects at least a hundred and thirty by the end of the year. Its chief executive has said data centers are expected to be about a third of its U.S. gas power deals. The machines GE built for a century are now powering the newest borrowing boom. Which brings us back to the bank. GE Capital didn't fail because lending is bad. It nearly failed because of a mismatch. It borrowed money that had to be renewed every few weeks, and lent it out for years. That works every day, until the day lenders hesitate. And on that day, it doesn't matter how big you are, or how many jet engines you make. Notice what saved GE. Not its factories. Not its brand. It was outside money, arriving fast: Buffett's capital, new shareholders, the Fed's program, and the FDIC's name. And notice what it cost. A diluted stock. A lost triple A rating. A decade of shrinking. And an insurance bill that arrived ten years after the crisis. The bank had made GE look stronger than it was, because the profits arrived every quarter, and the risk only showed up when the funding did not. If you watched our last video, you know the AI build-out is being paid for with debt too. Different structure, same question. Who is lending, for how long, and what happens if they stop?

GE survived. Buffett got his dividends. The government's guarantee was there when it was needed. But it took fifteen years, a lost credit rating, three dividend cuts and a breakup to undo what one borrowing machine had built. So here's my question for you. Was GE Capital a genius idea that went too far, or a risk that was always hiding in plain sight? Tell me in the comments. If you want more stories like this, built from the filings, subscribe. Next, we go back twenty-five years, to the company that made the word Enron mean fraud. And to the people who actually lost the money.
